MCP currently provides no native protocol mechanism to enforce where connected tools run or where data may be processed. Enterprise Exposure Through Consumer Networks 0.45% of analyzed hostnames were associated with home networks or consumer tunneling tools. AI agent workflows can connect to infrastructure outside traditional corporate network controls, creating visibility and governance gaps. Low-Cost Domain Takeover Paths 2.3% of hostnames failed to resolve , including six unregistered domains available for as little as $4 per year . Neatsun Ziv September 16, 2026 5 mins read Share AI agents are rapidly evolving toward more autonomy, more context, greater reach and more authority to act. We have to build security now for what’s coming next. We are making enormous bets right now about how to secure software two years from now, at exactly the moment when software is changing too quickly for anyone to know what it will look like. Every few months there is a new agent architecture, framework or standard. By 2028, many of the technologies we are designing for today will have changed dramatically or disappeared altogether. But we can’t wait until then to find out what survives. We have to make security decisions now for a software landscape we can’t yet see. This is what happens during a period of rapid evolution. New species appear quickly, most disappear, and over time the traits that give some of them an advantage begin to define what comes next. The jellyfish, the frog and the brain Most of the software running in companies today belongs to the old species. It is, in evolutionary terms, a jellyfish: sensors wired to reflexes, with no brain making a decision in the middle. A developer decides what should happen and writes that decision into code. Later, a request comes in, a pre-wired path fires and a response goes out. The jellyfish is not a failed organism. It has survived for more than 500 million years and will probably outlive us. Deterministic software isn’t going away either. There are many jobs for which predictable reflexes are exactly what we want. What we are building now is different. We have started giving software a brain, though in most cases the brain is not fully in charge – yet. We put an LLM inside a workflow, connect an agent to a defined set of tools or add intelligence to an application whose basic architecture was designed around predetermined paths. The software can reason about parts of the problem, but the old reflexes still determine much of what happens. I think of this as the frog in agentic evolution: part of the old world and part of the new one. The frog matters because it tells us a transition is underway. We don’t know what the next species will look like, but we can already see one of the most important traits it will need to survive: the brain will play an increasingly central role in determining what the system actually does. That is where I think much of the industry is making a mistake. We are designing security around the agents, frameworks and architectures that happen to exist today, rather than the capabilities that are likely to survive them. Today’s agent architectures are transitional species. Some will evolve; some will occupy useful niches for a long time; others will disappear. If we’re building security now for systems that have to remain relevant years from now, the frog cannot be our design target. What the frog teaches us should be. Bet on the traits, not the species What we can already see in this period of “agentic Darwinism” is that the locus of decision-making is moving toward the brain. As software gains memory, autonomy, access to tools and data, and the authority to act, intelligence stops being a feature inside a predetermined flow and starts determining the flow itself. Context and memory inform the decision. Tools give the system ways to act. Identity gives it authority. The path emerges from the decision instead of being completely laid down in advance. As a result, more of an application’s behavior is determined at runtime. Developers increasingly define the capabilities and boundaries of a system without knowing every path it will take inside them.
